prompt: While it processes TK-4471 only on Tarefa's instructions, what is the model provider under the LGPD?
hint: Who decides why the ticket is processed?

choices.text: The controller, because the model and the computers are its own
choices.why: Owning the machines does not make it the controller; deciding the purpose does, and Tarefa decides it.

choices.text: The processor, handling the data on Tarefa's behalf
choices.why: Right: an operador, bound by art. 39 to follow the controller's instructions.

choices.text: The encarregado, the one named for data-protection questions
choices.why: The encarregado is a person the controller names, not the company it sends data to.

choices.text: Nobody in particular, since it only passes data through
choices.why: Transferring and communicating data are processing under art. 5, X.

prompt: A provider's terms say prompts may be used to improve its models, and Tarefa's plan cannot turn that off. What does that change?
hint: Who is deciding the purpose of that use?

choices.text: Nothing, because a processor may use what it receives to improve the service it sells
choices.why: A processor processes on the controller's instructions; improving its own models is not one of Tarefa's.

choices.text: It decides a purpose of its own, as a controller does, and the notice must say so
choices.why: Right: for that use it is no longer only an operador, and the people in the tickets have to be told.

choices.text: The prompts stop being personal data once they are used for training
choices.why: Training does not anonymise anything; the prompts are as personal as they were.

choices.text: Tarefa becomes the processor and the provider the controller of the whole call
choices.why: Tarefa still decides why the ticket is summarised; only the training use changes hands.

prompt: Which of these does the LGPD treat as personal data, from Tarefa's point of view? Choose all that apply.
hint: Identified or identifiable, art. 5, I.

choices.text: The freelancer's Pix key
choices.why: Yes: it is her e-mail address, and it identifies her.

choices.text: The message "Call me on +55 11 98765-4321"
choices.why: Yes: a phone number identifies its owner as well as a name does.

choices.text: The client's birth date
choices.why: Yes: information about an identified person.

choices.text: The messages after the names are replaced by placeholders
choices.why: Tarefa holds the vault that reverses them, so for Tarefa they are still personal data.

prompt: Why does sending the ticket to a model that runs outside Brazil need one of the mechanisms in art. 33?
hint: Where is the data going?

choices.text: Art. 33 applies only when the data includes sensitive data
choices.why: It applies to any personal data that leaves the country.

choices.text: Each provider has to be approved by the ANPD before its first call
choices.why: There is no such approval; the controller provides the guarantees, usually by contract.

choices.text: Because it is an international transfer of personal data
choices.why: Right: and art. 33 lists the cases in which one is allowed.

choices.text: Because each data subject must consent to it, in every case
choices.why: Consent is one of the cases listed, not a requirement for all of them; contracts with the standard clauses are the common route.

prompt: Match each principle of art. 6 to what it asks of the summary feature.
hint: One description on the right belongs to no principle.

pairs.right: Process the ticket for a stated, specific purpose
Send only the fields that purpose requires
Tell the people in the ticket that a provider reads it
Protect the outbox and the vault from unauthorised access

right_distractors: Ask for consent before every single call

prompt: Why does a purpose that lists the fields it needs apply the necessity principle better than a list of fields to remove?
hint: Think about the field somebody adds to the ticket next year.

choices.text: The LGPD forbids writing the purpose as a list of fields to remove
choices.why: The law says nothing about how the list is written; the difference is what happens to a new field.

choices.text: A field nobody listed is dropped without anyone having to remember it
choices.why: Right: a new field added to the ticket stays at home until somebody argues it in.

choices.text: A short list of needed fields makes each request cheaper
choices.why: It does, and that is a side effect, not why it applies the principle.

choices.text: Providers reject any request that carries fields they do not know
choices.why: A model reads whatever it is sent; nothing rejects the extra fields.

prompt: How many fields does `guard minimise` list as dropped for TK-4471?
hint: Count the names after `dropped`.

prompt: For Tarefa, is the minimised outbox anonymised data under art. 12?
hint: Can Tarefa turn it back into names?

choices.text: Yes, because the provider has no way of reversing it
choices.why: The question is about Tarefa, which holds the vault.

choices.text: Yes, once the placeholders are numbered afresh in every ticket
choices.why: Numbering changes nothing; the vault still maps each placeholder back.

choices.text: No: the vault reverses it, so it stays personal data
choices.why: Right: art. 13, §4 is the definition, and pseudonymised data keeps every obligation.

choices.text: No, because a job title such as a logo for a bakery is a name
choices.why: A job title is not a name; the vault is what makes the outbox reversible.

prompt: Lesson 21 said no pattern finds a name. How did `guard minimise` find "Juliana" inside a message?
hint: What does the ticket already say about its people?

choices.text: A model inside the tool recognises people's names
choices.why: There is no model in the lab; the tool reads Python's standard library and nothing else.

choices.text: It replaces every capitalised word that is not at the start of a sentence
choices.why: That would replace September, and it did not.

choices.text: The ticket's own fields hold the names, so it searched for those words
choices.why: Right: it knew what to look for, first names included, and a third person mentioned only in a message would get through.

choices.text: The client typed the name into a field marked as a name
choices.why: The client typed it into a message, which is free text.

prompt: `guard restore` puts the names back using the ___, the one file that never leaves Tarefa's machine.
hint: It is written beside the outbox, under a folder of its own.

prompt: Which of these could still lead back to a person from the outbox? Choose all that apply.
hint: Minimisation lowers the risk without reaching zero.

choices.text: The ticket number TK-4471, for anybody with access to Tarefa's database
choices.why: Yes: it is a key to the full ticket.

choices.text: A late logo for a bakery, an amount and a date, in a small town
choices.why: Yes: few bakeries may fit, and that is enough.

choices.text: A lawyer named only inside one of the messages
choices.why: Yes: the tool looks for the names the ticket's fields hold, and a third person is not one of them.

choices.text: <PHONE_1>, for the provider that receives it
choices.why: The provider has no vault; the placeholder means nothing to it.

prompt: Why can't Tarefa use legitimate interest as the basis for sending Juliana's health information to the provider?
hint: Which article governs sensitive data?

choices.text: Legitimate interest is a basis that only public bodies may use
choices.why: Private companies use it all the time, for ordinary personal data.

choices.text: Art. 11, the list for sensitive data, leaves it out
choices.why: Right: its list is shorter than art. 7's, and legitimate interest is not on it.

choices.text: Health data cannot be processed under the LGPD on any basis
choices.why: It can, on the bases art. 11 lists.

choices.text: Legitimate interest needs the ANPD's approval for each case
choices.why: No approval is needed; it is simply not available for sensitive data.

prompt: Why does `guard minimise --sensitive remove` leave a marker where the sentence was, instead of deleting it without a trace?
hint: Read the summary the course wrote for the reply.

choices.text: So the provider can ask Tarefa for the removed sentence if it needs it
choices.why: The provider never gets the sentence; the marker is for the model reading the message.

choices.text: So the model knows a reason was given, and the summary stays fair
choices.why: Right: without it she reads as late with no explanation.

choices.text: Because the LGPD requires every removal of data to be marked in the text
choices.why: No such rule; the marker is a choice about the summary's quality.

choices.text: So that `guard restore` can put the sentence back into the reply
choices.why: The sentence is not in the vault; nothing puts it back.

prompt: Which of these messages would the lab's word list let through to the provider unchanged? Choose all that apply.
hint: The list sees words, not meaning.

choices.text: I spent a week in bed with a fever and the doctor said rest
choices.why: Yes: illness without any word on the list.

choices.text: My son has autism and I can only work at night
choices.why: Yes: a third party's health, and the list has never heard of autism.

choices.text: I was in hospital for a week with a kidney infection
choices.why: Caught: hospital and infection are both on the list.

choices.text: The medication I take makes me slow in the mornings
choices.why: Caught: medication is on the list.

prompt: Health is a common reason in Tarefa's disputes, and the word list misses many of them. Which change does the lesson favour?
hint: Where is the data safest: filtered, or never collected?

choices.text: Grow the word list until no health message gets through
choices.why: A longer list moves the line and leaves it in place.

choices.text: Ask the model to strip health details before it summarises
choices.why: By then the message is already at the provider; the data has left.

choices.text: Ask for a category, not free text, and route those cases to a person
choices.why: Right: a category is all the dispute needs, and a person reads the cases the model should not.

choices.text: Collect a consent for health data from freelancers when they sign up
choices.why: Art. 11 wants consent that is specific to a purpose; a blanket form at signup is weak ground.

prompt: Why does the contract need a clause on how fast the provider reports a security incident to Tarefa?
hint: Who notifies the ANPD, and by when?

choices.text: The provider notifies the ANPD itself, as the party that suffered the incident
choices.why: Tarefa is the controller; notifying the ANPD and the data subjects is its duty, wherever the incident happened.

choices.text: Incidents at a processor fall outside the LGPD
choices.why: They are the controller's incidents too.

choices.text: Tarefa has three working days to notify the ANPD, and needs to hear fast
choices.why: Right: Resolution CD/ANPD nº 15 of 2024 sets the three working days.

choices.text: The ANPD deadline is whatever the contract sets
choices.why: The deadline is the ANPD's; the contract only decides whether Tarefa can meet it.

prompt: Match each right in art. 18 to what it asks of the summary feature.
hint: One answer on the right is not a right at all.

pairs.right: Say that a model provider receives the tickets
Delete the ticket, its logs and its vault
Fix a wrong summary saved in the ticket

right_distractors: Stop the provider from billing for the call

prompt: How many working days does Resolution CD/ANPD nº 15 of 2024 give the controller to notify the ANPD of an incident?
hint: The section says it in words.

prompt: Put the life of one ticket through the summary feature in order.
hint: The provider sees only the middle of it.
items: Minimise the ticket and write the vault
Send the outbox to the provider
Receive a reply that uses the placeholders
Restore the names before the agent reads it

prompt: Juliana asks Tarefa to delete her data after the dispute closes. Tarefa deletes the ticket and its logs and keeps `vault/TK-4471.json`. What is wrong?
hint: What is the vault the key to?

choices.text: Nothing, since the vault holds placeholders and not personal data
choices.why: It holds exactly the personal data: each placeholder beside the name it hides.

choices.text: The vault should go to the provider so it can delete its own copy
choices.why: The vault must never leave Tarefa; sending it would hand over the names.

choices.text: The copy at the provider is what matters here, because the vault never left Tarefa
choices.why: The provider's copy is one problem; the vault is a second one, at home.

choices.text: The vault turns the outbox back into names, so the ticket can be rebuilt
choices.why: Right: it has to be deleted with the ticket, or the deletion is incomplete.
